32 What is a possible charge on a particle?
A
6.40  10–20
C
B
4.00  10–19
C
C
1.12  10–18
C
D
9.11  10–18
C

hints: Notice all four options are charges in $\text{C}$ of order $10^{-20}$ to $10^{-18}$ - compare each to the elementary charge $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$.
Recall charge is quantised, so an isolated particle must have $Q = ne$ where $n$ is an integer - test this with $n = Q/e$.
Calculate $Q/(1.60 \times 10^{-19})$ for each option and look for the one that gives a whole number, here $1.12 \times 10^{-18} / 1.60 \times 10^{-19} = 7$.
walkthrough: Identify the rule: charge on matter is quantised in multiples of the elementary charge $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, so $Q = ne$ with integer $n$.
Rearrange to test each value: $n = Q/e = Q/(1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C})$. Only an integer $n$ is possible.
Test option A: $n = 6.40 \times 10^{-20} / 1.60 \times 10^{-19} = 0.40$, not an integer.
Test option B: $n = 4.00 \times 10^{-19} / 1.60 \times 10^{-19} = 2.5$, not an integer.
Test option C: $n = 1.12 \times 10^{-18} / 1.60 \times 10^{-19} = 11.2/1.6 = 7.0$, which is an integer.
Test option D for completeness: $n = 9.11 \times 10^{-18} / 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \approx 56.9$, not an integer.
Only the $7e$ value satisfies quantisation. This is option C.

A.explanation: Dividing $6.40 \times 10^{-20}$ by $1.60 \times 10^{-19}$ gives $0.40e$, which is not an integer multiple of the elementary charge.

B.explanation: Dividing $4.00 \times 10^{-19}$ by $1.60 \times 10^{-19}$ gives $2.5e$, which is not an integer number of elementary charges.

C.explanation: Dividing $1.12 \times 10^{-18}$ by $1.60 \times 10^{-19}$ gives exactly $7e$, an integer multiple of the elementary charge.

D.explanation: Dividing $9.11 \times 10^{-18}$ by $1.60 \times 10^{-19}$ gives about $56.9e$, which is not an integer multiple of the elementary charge.
